newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets edgy in final hours of compaign.
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets edgy in final hours of compaign.

text.p: With President Bill Clinton still in front in pre-election polls but with a narrower lead, U.S. financial markets have grown increasingly nervous about the possibilty the Democrats will continue to occupy the White House and regain control of the House of Representatives.
"It's generally accepted that Clinton is going to win the presidency," Hugh Johnson, strategist at First Albany Co., said Sunday.
"From Wall Street's perspective, the concern is, 'What's going to happen in the House of Representatives.?'"

Johnson said the concern and focus on Wall Street centered on the possiblity that progress in reducing the U.S. budget deficit would be slowed or halted should Clinton continue in the White House without the counterweight of a House of Representatives controlled by his political opponents.
Most experts say the Republicans are likely to retain their control of the U.S. Senate.

Johnson said Wall Street's fixation on the budget is so intense that there could even be a negative market reaction if Republican challenger Bob Dole pulled off a major upset and defeated Clinton. Dole's talk of a tax cut is the reason for the concern, he said.
The focus on the congressional races underscored the fact that the presidential contest has settled into a repetitive back-and-forth, sparring over such issues as health care and Clinton's ethics.

On NBC's Meet the Press television program Sunday, Republican national chairman Haley Barbour and Democratic chairman Sen. Christopher Dodd dueled over the issue of campaign financing. Republicans have been hammering away lately, with accusations about flows of foreign money to the Democratic campaign.
Despite the polls showing Clinton in front, one question was how voter apathy would affect the actual result when the polls open on Tuesday.

"It's been a boring campaign," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist a Dean Witter Reynolds. He cited one poll showing that only one-half of registered voters were likely to exercise their right to vote.

But he noted that U.S. markets have been pre-occupied with the election in the last few weeks. Economic news Friday showing a moderate economy with a 5.2 percent jobless rate amid subdued inflation ordinarily would have caused stock to rally, Canelo said. Instead, investors stayed on the sidelines, evidently content to wait until after the election before making major new commitments.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended with a small loss Friday, falling seven points to 6,022.

Canelo said heading into the final hours of the campaign, the signs were pointing to a continuation of the "status quo" with Clinton likely to be re-elected and and the Republicans likely to hold onto a majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
That, he said, would be the outcome most pleasing to investors.

He noted that most of the gains on Wall Street during Clinton's four years in office have occurred in the two years since the Republicans won control of both the House and Senate in the 1994 election.
For investors trying to decide in advance which way the markets might move Wednesday morning, one wild card is a ballot initiative known as Proposition 211 in California.

Proponents say the measure, which would make it easier to file class action securities lawsuits in state court, would make corporations more accountable and deter financial fraud. It opponents argue that it would have a chilling effect on the dissemination of forward-looking information to investors.
Should the measure pass, Johnson said, "it will seriously in my view interrupt the free flow of information from companies to research analysts, or for that matter, investors."
He said if Proposition 211 is approved, it would upset investors, especially because companies other than those based in California would be affected.

Robert Stovall, a market strategist with Stovall/Twenty-First Advisers, said a look at market history and past political contests suggests 1997 could be a troublesome year. The stock market "definitely goes down in the year after a president is re-elected," he said.
In 1937, for example, the market collapsed after Franklin Roosevelt was re-elected, Stovall noted. The only glaring exception to this phenomenon was in the second term of Ronald Reagan.

Another ominous sign, Stovall said, is the third-party candidacy of Ross Perot. With few exceptions, such third-party efforts signal a certain unrest among the electorate that has a correlation with ensuing bear markets, he said.
Stovall, who is cautiously optimistic on the outlook for further gains in the stock market, said: "We should still see an up year in 1997, but working against it is a lot of negative precedent."
Two days before the election, the bottom line, he said, is that "there is all kinds of speculation about what would happen if the Democrats ran everything."
